1.

This award shall decide the claim petition filed on the basis of the Detailed Accident Report (DAR)
seeking compensation on account of the death of the husband of petitioner No.1 and father of the petitioners No. 2 to 5 in a road traffic accident.

2. In brief, the facts as narrated in the FIR are that on 20-21.02.2018 at about 05:00 am, Bhu Dayal (since deceased) was proceeding from Paper Market side to Hindon Pul on his bicycle (fruit bucket attached to carrier).

At the same time one car bearing registration No. DL-1Z-3472, came from the same direction, driven by respondent No.1 at a very high speed; in a rash and negligent manner and Mithlesh vs Rakesh on 4 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/83016497/
1 hit the deceased.
As a result, the bicycle rider fell down on road about 8-10 meters away and sustained grievous injuries.
It is further stated that after the accident, PCR and CAT ambulance services were called at the spot.
The CAT ambulance staff, after examining Bhu Dayal, declared him dead.
The driver of the offending vehicle was apprehended by the patrolling staff near Murga Mandi cut who was deputed at the place of occurrence after chasing the vehicle.
In connection with the accident, FIR No. 0060/2018 was registered at Police Station- Ghazipur.
3. Both respondents entered appearance; however, despite opportunities granted, they failed to file their written statements.
Consequently, their right to file written statement(s) was struck off by the order dated 03.11.2018, and the matter was ordered to be proceeded ex parte for the petitioner's evidence.
4. In order to establish their claim, the petitioners examined two witnesses.
5. The petitioner No.1 - Mithlesh (PW1), stepped into the witness box and tendered her evidence by way of affidavit Ex.PW1/A.
She deposed about the manner of the accident and the involvement of the offending vehicle.

She relied upon the following documents:
a) DAR - Ex.PW1/1 (colly)
b) Copy of her aadhar card - Ex.PW1/2 (OSR)
c) Copy of death certificates of deceased - Ex.PW1/3 (OSR)
6.
PW1 was duly cross-examined by the Ld. Counsel for the respondents.

7. PW2- Retired ASI Banwari Lal was examined as an eye-witness to the accident, who relied upon the complaint Ex.PW2/A.
8.
The respondents did not choose to lead any evidence on their behalf.
9. This Tribunal has heard Sh. A.K. Mishra, Ld. Counsel for petitioners.
No-one has come forward to address arguments on behalf of respondents.
The record of the case has also been perused.
INVOLVEMENT AND RASH AND NEGLIGENCE OF THE OFFENDING VEHICLE:
10. In an action founded on the principle of fault liability, proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.

However, the standard of proof is not as strict as that applied in criminal cases and in fact, the preponderance of probabilities which is mandate in civil cases governs proceedings before the tribunal.
It is also well settled that the Tribunal is not bound by the technical rules of evidence.
Further, holding any inquiry under section 168 of the Motor Vehicles Act, while the Claims Tribunal may follow such summary procedure as it deems fit.
11. In order to prove their case, the petitioners examined two witnesses.
PW1 tendered her testimony by way of affidavit Ex.PW1/A.

In order to prove the manner of the accident, the petitioners Mithlesh vs Rakesh on 4 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/83016497/
2 examined PW2 - Retired ASI Banwari Lal, who was an eye witness to the incident.

He deposed that in the intervening night of 20-21.02.2018, he was on duty on ERV vehicle bearing No.
DL-1CM-4026 from 8:00 am to 8:00 pm.

He further stated that at about 5;00 am, while he was standing at Canal Hindon near the bridge, a bicycle rider came from the Paper Market side carrying a fruit basket on his bicycle and was going towards Murga Mandi Side.
At that time, vehicle bearing registration No.DL-1Z-2472, which was also coming from the paper Market side was driven by its driver in a rash and negligent manner and hit the cyclist.

He further deposed that due to the impact,
the cyclist fell down and sustained grievous injuries, and the driver of the offending vehicle fled towards Murga Mandi alongwith the vehicle.
12. He further deposed that he has already deposed in the connected FIR case No. 60/18 PS Ghazipur, as an eye-witness.

He further stated that he handed over the accused Rakesh to the IO /
ASI Dharamveer Singh.
PW1 was not cross
- examined by the respondents and his testimony remained unassailed and unchallenged.
It is further noted that the FIR regarding the accident was registered on the very next day of the date of occurrence.

13. It is further not in dispute that respondent No.1/driver Rakesh was charge-sheeted in the aforesaid criminal case for causing the accident by driving the offending vehicle in a rash and negligent manner.
Thus, prima-facie, it is clear that respondent No.1 was driving the offending vehicle in a rash and negligent manner at the time of accident.
14. After investigation, the police filed a charge-sheet against respondent no. 1, the driver of the offending car.
The filing of the charge-sheet against the driver of the offending vehicle prima-facie establishes his culpability.

In this regard, reliance is placed on the judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of New India Assurance Company Ltd vs Smt. Washeema Bano (2022)
SCC OnLine All 403 and Mangla Ram vs Oriental Insurance Company Ltd (2018) 5SCC 656),
wherein it was held that filing of a charge-sheet against the driver of the offending vehicle constitutes prima facie evidence of negligence for the purpose of claim under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.

Accordingly, issue no.1 is decided in favour of the petitioner and against the respondents.
COMPUTATION OF COMPENSATION:

19. Section 168 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 enjoins upon the claim Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation, which appears to be just and reasonable.
As per the settled law, compensation is not expected to be windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance.
A man is not compensated for the physical injury, he is compensated for the loss which he suffers as a result of that injury (Baker v. Willoughby (1970) Ac 467 at page 492 per Lord Reid).

20. In death cases, the guidelines for computation of compensation have been laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case of Sarla Verma and Others v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr. (2009) 6 Supreme Court Cases 121.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Further, the guidelines have been reiterated by the Constitution Bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in a case titled as National Insurance Company vs. Pranay Sethi & Ors.,
decided on 31.10.2017, laying down the general principles for computation of compensation in death cases.

entities.text: National Insurance Company vs. Pranay Sethi & Ors
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant paras of the judgment are reproduced here as under:
"18.
If these determinations are standardized, there will be uniformity and consistency in the decisions.
There will be lesser need for detailed evidence.
It will also be easier for the insurance companies to settle accident claims without delay.
19. To have uniformity and consistency, the Tribunals should determine compensation in cases of death, by the following well-settled steps: death case Step-1 (Ascertaining the multiplicand)
The income of the deceased per annum should be determined.
Out of the said income a deduction should be made in regard to the amount which the deceased would have spent on himself by way of personal and living expenses.
The balance expired e which is considered to be the contribution to the dependent family, constitutes the multiplicand.
Step-2 (Ascertaining the multiplier) death case
Having regard to the age of the deceased and period of active career, the appropriate multiplier should be selected.
This does not mean ascertaining the number of years he would have lived or worked but for the accident.
Having regard to several imponderables in life and economic factors, a table of multipliers with reference to the age has been identified by this Court.
The multiplier should be chosen from the said table with reference to the age of the deceased.
Step-3 (Actual Calculation)
The annual contribution to the family(multiplicand) when multiplied by such multiplier gives the 'loss of dependency' to the family.
Thereafter, a conventional amount in the range of Rs.5,000/- to Rs.10,000/- may be added as loss of estates.
Where the deceased is survived by his widow, another conventional amount in the range of Rs.5,000 to Rs.10,000 should be added under the head of loss of consortium.
But no amount is to be awarded under the head of pain, suffering or hardship caused to the legal heirs of the deceased.
The funeral expenses, cost of transportation of the body (if incurred) and the cost of any medical treatment of the deceased before death (if incurred) should also be added."

Therefore, in view of the aforesaid judgment, it is essential to take into consideration the following parameters:-
PECUNIARY DAMAGES:
A. Age of deceased :
21.
As per the Aadhar Card of the deceased, his date of birth is 01.01.1970.
The date of accident is 21.02.2018.
Thus, the age of the deceased was 48 years and 1 month at the time of accident.

B. Assessment of Income of deceased :
22. PW1 / petitioner No.1, who is the wife of the deceased testified in her examination-in-chief (Ex.PW1/A) that her deceased husband was working as a fruit Mithlesh vs Rakesh on 4 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/83016497/
5 vendor and was earning more than Rs.22,000/- per month.
However, in order to substantiate this contention, the petitioner No.1 has not produced any documentary evidence.
As per the Aadhaar Card, the deceased was stated to be a resident of Uttar Pradesh.
No documentary evidence has been led by PW1 regarding the actual income of the deceased.
In the testimony of PW1, it is nowhere mentioned that the deceased was working in Delhi.
No educational documents of the deceased have been proved on record either.

Hence, in the considered view of this Tribunal, the income of the deceased Sh. Bhu Dayal has to be taken as per the minimum wages applicable to an unskilled worker prevalent in the State of Uttar Pradesh and at the time of the death of deceased; the same was Rs.7,400/- per month.
Thus, the income of the deceased is considered to be Rs.7,400/- per month.

C. Number of dependents :
23.

In the DAR claim filed by the Investigating Officer, there are five petitioners /
legal heirs of the deceased, namely the wife and children of the deceased.
All the children are apparently major on the date of the accident.
As per the testimony of PW1, it has nowhere come on record that the petitioner No. 2 to 4, who are the children of the deceased were dependents upon him.
No specific evidence has been brought on record to substantiate the claim of the petitioners that all the petitioners were dependents of the deceased.
In the absence of any specific evidence regarding dependency on the deceased, it can be assumed that all the children of the deceased are not dependent upon him.
Thus, the children of the deceased are not considered dependents on the deceased and only the wife is considered as his dependent.

D.
Application of Multiplier:
24.
As discussed above, the deceased was 48 years and 1 month of age at the time of the accident.
An appropriate multiplier has to be determined for computation of compensation.
The judgment titled as Sarla Verma v. DTC (2009) 6 SCC 121 is relevant to consider the multiplier.

In Para 21 of the judgment, the guidelines for the multiplier were laid down in accordance with age are as under:-

E. Future Prospects:
26.
This issue was considered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Pranay Sethi & Others (Supra).

Relevant parts of the judgment are reproduced here as under:
"(iii) While determining the income, an addition of 50% of actual salary to the income of the deceased towards future prospects, where the deceased had a permanent job and was below the age of 40 years, should be made.
The addition should be 30%, if the age of the deceased was between 40 to 50 years.
In case the deceased was between the age of 50 to 60 years, the addition should be 15%.
Actual salary should be read as actual salary less tax.
(iv) In case the deceased was self-employed or on a fixed salary, an addition of 40% of the established income should be the warrant where the deceased was below the age of 40 years.
An addition of 25% where the deceased was between the age of 40 to 50 years and 10% where the deceased was between the age of 50 to 60 years should be regarded as the necessary method of computation.
The established income means the income minus the tax component."
27. The deceased can be considered a self-employed.

In view of the above said judgment, the deceased, who was 48 years and 1 month of age, an addition of income of deceased to the extent of 25% has to be considered in view of decision of a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in the case, National Insurance Company Ltd. Vs. Pranay Sethi and Ors.

After choosing the age, multiplier and income of the deceased, necessary deductions have to be made out of the income of the deceased towards his personal expenses.

31.

LIABILITY;
34.
The next question that arises for consideration is as to which of the respondents is liable to pay the said compensation amount.
It is an admittedly fact that the offending vehicle was not insured on the date of accident.
Respondent No.1 was the driver of the vehicle and was driving the same at the time of accident while respondent No.2 was the registered owner of the offending vehicle.
The liability of the driver (Respondent No. 1), the registered owner (Respondent No.2) are held jointly and severally.
Thus, respondents No.1 and 2 are jointly and severally liable to pay the compensation to the petitioner.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as that applied in criminal cases and in fact, the preponderance of probabilities which is mandate in civil cases governs proceedings before the tribunal.
14. After investigation, the police filed a charge-sheet against respondent no. 1, the driver of the offending car.
The filing of the charge-sheet against the driver of the offending vehicle prima-facie establishes his culpability.
In this regard, reliance is placed on the judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of New India Assurance Company Ltd vs Smt. Washeema Bano (2022)
SCC OnLine All 403 and Mangla Ram vs Oriental Insurance Company Ltd (2018) 5SCC 656),
wherein it was held that filing of a charge-sheet against the driver of the offending vehicle constitutes prima facie evidence of negligence for the purpose of claim under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.
15. In New India Assurance Company Ltd vs Pazhaniammal (2011) (2) KLT 648, the Hon'ble High Court of Kerala has held that, as a general rule, production of charge-sheet can be accepted as prima-facie sufficient evidence of negligence in claim proceedings under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act.
However, if any party disputes, the burden lies on such party to adduce evidence in rebuttal.
If the Tribunal finds that charge-sheet appears collusive, it may discard the same and call upon the parties to lead oral evidence of accident and alleged negligence.
Thus, the issue of negligence must be decided based on the entirety of evidence on record.
In the case of Cholamandalam MS General Insurance Company Ltd vs Smt. Kamlesh and Others 2009 (3) AD Delhi 310 it was held that an adverse inference can be drawn when the driver of the offending vehicle does not enter into the witness box.
Mithlesh vs Rakesh on 4 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/83016497/

Accordingly, issue no.1 is decided in favour of the petitioner and against the respondents.
As per the settled law, compensation is not expected to be windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance.
A man is not compensated for the physical injury, he is compensated for the loss which he suffers as a result of that injury (Baker v. Willoughby (1970) Ac 467 at page 492 per Lord Reid).
20. In death cases, the guidelines for computation of compensation have been laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case of Sarla Verma and Others v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr. (2009) 6 Supreme Court Cases 121.
The income of the deceased per annum should be determined.
No documentary evidence has been led by PW1 regarding the actual income of the deceased.
In the testimony of PW1, it is nowhere mentioned that the deceased was working in Delhi.
No educational documents of the deceased have been proved on record either.
Hence, in the considered view of this Tribunal, the income of the deceased Sh. Bhu Dayal has to be taken as per the minimum wages applicable to an unskilled worker prevalent in the State of Uttar Pradesh and at the time of the death of deceased; the same was Rs.7,400/- per month.
All the children are apparently major on the date of the accident.
As per the testimony of PW1, it has nowhere come on record that the petitioner No. 2 to 4, who are the children of the deceased were dependents upon him.
No specific evidence has been brought on record to substantiate the claim of the petitioners that all the petitioners were dependents of the deceased.
In the absence of any specific evidence regarding dependency on the deceased, it can be assumed that all the children of the deceased are not dependent upon him.
Thus, the children of the deceased are not considered dependents on the deceased and only the wife is considered as his dependent.
In view of the above said judgment, the deceased, who was 48 years and 1 month of age, an addition of income of deceased to the extent of 25% has to be considered in view of decision of a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in the case, National Insurance Company Ltd. Vs. Pranay Sethi and Ors.
Further, in view of recent decision of Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case titled as United India Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Satinder Kaur @
Satwinder Kaur & Ors., Civil Appeal no. 2705 of 2020, decided on 30.06.2020, loss of consortium has to be fixed for each of the LRs.
It is an admittedly fact that the offending vehicle was not insured on the date of accident.
Respondent No.1 was the driver of the vehicle and was driving the same at the time of accident while respondent No.2 was the registered owner of the offending vehicle.
